evidence.quote: Fifteen men with a history of suicidal and aggressive behaviors and a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder and/or antisocial personality disorder participated in semistructured interviews that consisted of questions about their mental health status and experiences with mental health and addiction services.
Eighteen men were approached and 15 men agreed to participate in the full study and met the study inclusion criteria.
recruitment efforts focused on outpatient settings within the University of Toronto psychiatric network

Fifteen men with a history of suicidal and aggressive behaviors and a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder and/or antisocial personality disorder participated in semistructured interviews that consisted of questions about their mental health status and experiences with mental health and addiction services.
Mental health service providers were asked to refer patients to the study if they met the following criteria: male, 18 years of age or more, a history of suicidal behavior

Fifteen men with a history of suicidal and aggressive behaviors and a diagnosis of borderline personality disorder and/or antisocial personality disorder participated in semistructured interviews that consisted of questions about their mental health status and experiences with mental health and addiction services. Interviews were taped and transcribed.
To address this gap in knowledge, we completed a study to examine health service access issues among suicidal men with substance use disorder or personality disorders.
A trained interviewer conducted face-to-face, audiotaped interviews that were transcribed verbatim.

Recovery: Past year health service use Visited family doctor 73%; Visited hospital emergency department 67%; Visited psychiatrist at least once 67%; Admitted to hospital for psychiatric reasons 40%; Joined outpatient group for people with histories of suicidal behavior 40%; Used telephone crisis support services 40%.

Men in our study spoke about experiencing fragmented pathways to mental health care, and they partly attributed the persistence of their mental health problems to what they viewed as irregular, infrequent, and unpleasant experiences with mental health service providers. Generally, men spoke about a cyclical pattern wherein negative experiences with health care providers were followed by avoidance of health care settings, crisis, and then by involuntary service utilization. Some went from one provider to another (e.g., emergency department, to crisis team, to assessment, to a family doctor) in search of care but were unable to acquire the type of help or referral they sought. This cyclical pattern tended to result in a deterioration of respect for service providers and a sense that they would not receive the help they needed. Specific provider practices, patient practices, and episodes (see Table 2) were noted to contribute to the fragmented pathways. In particular, men identified three personal practices, five health-care provider practices and two types of episodes they believed contributed to their fragmented pathways to care. While the practices and episodes have been separated conceptually, in the sections to follow we attempt to provide a sense of how they interconnect in reality. Table 2. Practices and episodes that contribute to fragment- ed pathways to care Patient practices Failure to identify or acknowledge mental health problems Inability to articulate feelings and emotions Difficulties navigating the referral system Provider practices Distress mislabeled Failure to identify or acknowledge underlying factors Disrespectful treatment of patients Insufficient assessment Overreliance on medications Episodes Use of drastic measures Experience indignities during hospitalization

Men may be unable to articulate emotion because they don't know how or believe that expressing emotion is not permissible for men. At the same time, men are in a dilemma of not being taken seriously if expressing their distress is considered "too behavioral" or "with inappropriate affect." This dilemma creates serious communication difficulties for patients and providers.Many life experiences led men in the study to have negative expectations of health care providers, and perhaps to feel that no help is available to them. Many struggle with a realization that they need help but fear that in seeking help they may have control taken away from them. These struggles may lead to delays in seeking help, unexpected or unwanted emergency department visits, and inpatient admissions. Our data also indicates that service providers in these settings are perceived to be disinterested about and hostile toward suicidal men with personality and/or substance use disorders, leading to some negative experiences.Anecdotally, many of the men in the study who joined a group intervention expressed hope for the future and some were able to begin more formal treatment program for their substance abuse.
